## The one-liner

> I integrated **5 data sources on crime, incarceration, poverty, race, and police spending** into **one dataset spanning 40 years, with entries for all 50 states**, in order to **assess the predictive power of crime rates, poverty rates, and racial diversity relative to incarceration rates across the United States and over time**; I found that **police spending was the most influential variable in creating these predictions**.


**Role:** I worked solo to independently build this project

**Repo:** [github.com/eskerani/prison-predictor-capstone](https://github.com/eskerani/prison-predictor-capstone)


## The question

Since the 1980s the United States' incarceration rate has skyrocketed; currently the US imprisons its citizens at one of the highest rates in the world. However, violent crime rates have been steadily falling since peaking in the 1990s. Thus, this project asks: **how do the predictive power of social factors (such as poverty, race, or government spending on police) compare to that of violent and property crime rates when using support vector regression to model the national incarceration rate?**

## The data

This project combines data from five sources, all of which are at the state level and contain information for the years 1980-2020:

* Data about the incarcerated population of each state (excluding federal prisoners) was obtained from the Bureau of Justice Statistics' Corrections Statistical Analysis Tool
* Crime data was downloaded from the FBI's Summary Reporting System (SRS)
* Data on police spending was collected by the Census Bureau and made available for download by the Urban Institute's State and Local Finance Data tool 
* Poverty data was collected by the Census Bureau and included the population of each state
* Race data was estimated based on demographic information included in the IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS)

Given the historical nature of this project, all data sets were ingested as one-time .csv or .xlsx downloads. Once downloaded, the datasets were individually cleaned and wrangled into a standardized format. The IPUMS data was aggregated up to the state and year level, at which point the datasets could be joined together using state and year as the key. Using these combined data, all features were standardized by population (per 100k) based on the population estimates originally included in the poverty dataset. **The resulting combined dataset contained 2,050 rows and 10 columns: state, year, total population, incarceration rate, total crime rate, violent crime rate, property crime rate, poverty rate, the rate of non-white residents, and police spending rate.** There were certainly some stumbling blocks along the way, especially because each data set came with its own caveats and quality issues that had to be resolved before the join could be carried out.

## The approach

This project uses support vector regression (SVR), chosen because of its ability to deal with complex, non-linear data while remaining more straightforward than methods such as XGBoost. Five single-variable models were trained, each using data from only one predictive factor to ensure that no other data affected predictions; in addition, one model was trained and tuned using all predictive factors as inputs in order to evaluate the importance of each factor when combined.

Three main evaluation metrics are used: correlation coefficient, R<sup>2</sup> score, and root mean squared error (RMSE). Additionally, permutation importance and SHAP values are used to determine the most influential feature of the final multi-variate model. Definitions of all metrics can be found in the writeup. 

## Findings

![Line plot displaying model predictions of the national incarceration rate over time using only police spending (in dotted green) and all features (in dashed orange) as inputs.](projects/capstone/all_graph.png)


Across the single-feature models, though none performed very well, police spending served as the best isolated predictor of national incarceration rates with an R<sup>2</sup> of 0.57 and an RMSE of 69.83. The combined model performed markedly better than any of the individual models (R<sup>2</sup> = 0.93, RMSE = 27.5 after tuning), indicating that accounting for more variables gives the model a much fuller picture of the factors that influence incarceration rates. Police spending was the most important feature in the combined model; its permutation feature importance was 0.24 and its SHAP value was 0.21. 

![A graph displaying each instance of each feature, that instance's value by color, and how that instance impacted the mode's predictions.](shap_graph.png)

The SHAP values also revealed the directionality of each variable's influence on the model's predictions. Lower police spending values drove incarceration rate predictions down, while higher spending drove them up. The poverty rate and non-white followed a similar trend, but this pattern was reversed for both types of crime: *lower* crime rates drove predictions *higher*, and vice versa. 

![A table displaying all evaluation metrics for each feature.](poster_table.png)

**These results indicate that the police spending rate has an important association with incarceration rates, but also that no single variable can adequately predict incarceration rates.** Organizations and individuals advocating for prison reform to combat mass incarceration should keep police spending in mind as a factor that could potentially influence incarceration rates. However, it must be noted that all data were based on survey estimates, and that to some extent these factors are inherently interrelated.
